items.title: Home
items.text:
Survives restarts. The state travels inside the message. Add Redis or Postgres when it outgrows the message or many people click at once.

Components V2 first. Build with containers, sections and galleries. A row of buttons is the simple case.

Typed all the way. risa passes pyright strict, so your editor knows every field.

Coming from miru? See what changes.

@risa.register(name="counter")
class Counter(risa.View):
    count: int = 0

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"Clicks: **{self.count}**"),
            ui.Row(ui.Button(self.click, label="+1")),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def click(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        self.count += 1
        await ctx.rerender()

Click it. In a real bot the count survives a restart, because it lives in the button itself.

items.title: Changelog
items.text: What changed in each release of hikari-risa.

items.title: Features
items.text:
• InStore(adopt=True) takes over the messages a view sent while it kept its state in the message: switch state= without raising the version, and the first click on an old message moves its state into the store. (#75)
  • MemoryStore(warn=False) turns off the warning add_view logs about a MemoryStore, for a bot that uses one on purpose. (#76)

The first release of hikari-risa, a component handler for hikari built for Components V2. It runs on Python 3.12 to 3.15 with hikari 2.5 or a later 2.x release.

  • A view is a class with fields, a render() and handlers. Its layout takes the components of a Components V2 message, such as buttons, selects, sections, galleries and containers, and a layout of action rows alone is a V1 message. Modals are not part of 1.0.
  • A view keeps its state in its own message by default, so a click still lands after a restart. InStore keeps it in memory, Redis, PostgreSQL or a store you write, with a time to live.
  • Handlers take arguments bound into the component and answer with respond, rerender, edit or replace. Auto-defer, once you turn it on, answers for a slow one in time.
  • Clicks on old messages fail closed: when the view changed in a way they cannot follow, they reach on_outdated, and when the stored state is gone, on_state_missing.
  • Dependency injection through linkd, shared with lightbulb, error handlers on the client, and both gateway and REST bots.
  • The hikari-risa command, also python -m risa, prints the versions of risa, Python and what risa installs for a bug report.

items.title: API reference
items.text:
A component handler for hikari, built on Discord's Components V2.

A view is a class whose fields are its state, whose render returns its layout, and whose handlers answer the clicks on it. The state travels inside the message by default, so views survive restarts with no infrastructure. A view that outgrows the message can keep its state in a store.

The names of risa.binding, risa.client, risa.context, risa.di, risa.errors, risa.state, risa.store and risa.view are also importable directly from risa.

items.text:
build(view: View) -> Rendered

Render view into the components of a new message, ready to send.

It runs the view's load, renders it, and writes an InStore view's first record. The result spreads into any hikari or lightbulb call that takes components=. If that send fails, the record stays behind until its TTL reaps it, or for good under InStore(ttl=None).

items.title: error_handler
items.text:
error_handler(func: T, /, *, priority: int = 0) -> T

error_handler(*, priority: int = 0) -> _ErrorHandlerDecorator

Register a function that answers clicks that failed.

@client.error_handler
async def on_error(failure: risa.ClickFailure) -> bool:
    if isinstance(failure.error, risa.StoreUnavailableError):
        await failure.ctx.respond("Try again in a moment.", ephemeral=True)
        return True
    return False

It runs when a handler, load, View.on_outdated or View.on_state_missing raises, or when the view's state cannot be reached before them; ClickFailure.stage says which. It returns True once it has dealt with the failure, and risa then logs nothing. Otherwise the next one runs, and if none returns True, risa logs the failure as it would without them. One that raises is logged and counts as False. Its parameters after the first are injected, as a handler's are. It runs without auto-defer, and Discord's three seconds count from the click, so a failure that comes late, such as a lock timeout, may leave it no time unless auto-defer answered first.

Parameters:

  • func (ErrorHandler | None, default: None ) –

    The function to register. Left out, the call takes priority and returns the decorator.

  • priority (int, default: 0 ) –

    Higher runs first; functions of one priority run in the order they were registered.

Returns:

  • ErrorHandler | _ErrorHandlerDecorator –

    The function, unchanged, or the decorator that registers one.

items.title: edit async
items.text:
edit(layout: Layout) -> None

Replace the message with layout, keeping the view's state on it.

For a screen the view's render does not draw, such as a confirmation or a closing message. A layout without interactive components ends the view, since nothing on it can be clicked any more. Like rerender(), it saves the view's state.

Parameters:

  • layout (Layout) –

    The new layout: one top-level component, or several in order.

Raises:

  • NoViewError –

    If the layout has interactive components and the view has durable fields, but this context has no view state, as in on_outdated and on_state_missing, or if replace() gave the message to another view.

  • EphemeralOriginError –

    If the message is ephemeral and the interaction was answered with a new message.

  • StateOverflowError –

    If an InMessage view's state does not fit the layout's components.

  • StateConflictError –

    If another process saved the view's state first. The view then holds that state.

  • StateUnreadableError –

    If another process saved the view's state first, in a form this code cannot read.

items.title: replace async
items.text:
replace(view: View) -> None

Turn the message into another view, which answers its clicks from here on.

It builds view as Client.build does, so a view in a store gets a record of its own. This view's state is not saved, also not when the handler returns, and its record stays until its ttl runs out. If the message cannot be edited, the new view's record stays the same way and this view keeps the message. Afterwards rerender() and edit() of this context raise NoViewError, since the message is no longer this view's; edit only ever shows this view's own components.

Parameters:

  • view (View) –

    The view to show, an instance of a registered class.

Raises:

  • EphemeralOriginError –

    If the message is ephemeral and the interaction was answered with a new message.

  • NotAViewError –

    If the view's class was never registered.

  • StateOverflowError –

    If an InMessage view's state does not fit its components.

  • ViewDeclarationError –

    If the view keeps its state in a store this client does not have.

items.title: rerender async
items.text:
rerender() -> None

Redraw the message from the view's current state, and save that state.

Every rerender is a commit. InMessage state is written into the message itself; InStore state goes to the store first, then the message is edited. A change made without calling it is saved when the handler returns, but that save can only log a failure; call it yourself, before any respond(), where a failure must be handled.

Raises:

  • NoViewError –

    If the view has durable fields but this context has no view state, as in on_outdated and on_state_missing, or if replace() gave the message to another view.

  • EphemeralOriginError –

    If the message is ephemeral and the interaction was answered with a new message.

  • StateOverflowError –

    If an InMessage view's state no longer fits its components.

  • StateConflictError –

    If another process saved the view's state first. The view then holds that state, so the handler can apply its change again and rerender.

  • StateUnreadableError –

    If another process saved the view's state first, in a form this code cannot read.

  • StateNotFoundError –

    If an InStore view's record disappeared while the handler ran.

items.title: View
items.text:
Bases: Struct

Base class of a view: a message's layout, its state, and the handlers behind it.

A view is a msgspec.Struct, and its annotated fields are its durable state, carried from click to click. Mark a field risa.Prop[...] to rebuild it fresh on every click instead, typically in load. Register the class with @risa.register, return its layout from render, and send it with client.build:

@risa.register(name="counter")
class Counter(risa.View):
    count: int = 0

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Row(ui.Button(self.add, label=f"Clicks: {self.count}"))

    @risa.handler
    async def add(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        self.count += 1
        await ctx.rerender()

Each click runs its handler on the latest saved state of its view, and clicks on one view queue up within a process, each waiting up to ten seconds for the lock; one that waits longer is logged and goes unanswered. A view without durable fields has nothing to protect and takes no lock, so its handlers may run at the same time. Across processes, an InStore view on a shared store lets the first write win, while for an InMessage view the last edit of the message wins. A change made without ctx.rerender() is saved when the handler returns, but that save can only log a failure, so a handler that must know calls ctx.rerender() itself, before any ctx.respond(). A handler that raises keeps what it saved through rerender() or edit() before, and loses the rest.

The default does nothing, so the click fails on the user's side, and risa logs it. Override it to answer the user, or to replace the dead message with ctx.edit(...) or ctx.replace(...). Its parameters are injected, as a handler's are, and ctx has no view state.

To answer clicks on one retired handler differently, keep a method with its id, version and wire parameters whose body says the component is outdated. It routes like any handler, and nothing is logged.

    *,
    handler_id: str | None = ...,
    version: int = ...,
    defer: AutoDefer | None = ...,

Make a view method a handler that components can route to.

Used bare it returns the handler, and with options a decorator that makes one. A handler takes the view and a ComponentContext, then its wire parameters, then anything to inject:

@risa.handler(defer=risa.AutoDefer.UPDATE)
async def vote(
    self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext, option: int, db: Database
) -> None: ...

Wire parameters come first, are positional, and are annotated bool, int, str, hikari.Snowflake or an enum.Enum of int or str values. They receive the values risa.bind put on the component. Every parameter after them without a default is injected through linkd, so a hikari enum such as hikari.ChannelType, which is not an enum.Enum, is injected too; to carry one on the wire, bind its value as an int. To inject an int or another of those types, default it to risa.INJECTED. A handler returns None.

Parameters:

    The view method to make a handler. Left out, the call takes options and returns the decorator.

  • handler_id (str | None, default: None ) –

    The id the handler routes under, the method's name by default. Pin it before renaming the method, so components already sent keep working.

  • version (int, default: 1 ) –

    Bump it when the wire parameters change. Components sent before keep routing to a method that still has the old version; once none does, they go to View.on_outdated.

  • defer (AutoDefer | None, default: None ) –

    The handler's AutoDefer, overriding the view's.

A client then routes it once it is passed to client.add_view, or without that if the client was made with use_global=True. The decorator raises ViewDeclarationError for a class risa cannot serve, such as a blank name, a prop without a default, or an InStore view without durable fields.

  • version (int, default: 1 ) –

items.title: InMessage
items.text:
InMessage(codec: Codec = BASE85)

Bases: Struct

Keep a view's durable state inside the message it renders.

The default placement. The state is written into the spare characters of the rendered components' custom_ids and read back from the message on every click. It needs no infrastructure, survives restarts, and lives exactly as long as the message. It is bounded by what the components can carry: up to about 70 bytes per interactive component with the default codec.

The state is readable by anyone who can see the message, so never keep secrets in durable fields. A click cannot change it: risa reads it from the message Discord delivers with the click.

A rerender that changes the state changes the custom_id of the buttons that carry it. In tests Discord refused a click on a custom_id the message no longer has, so someone whose client still shows the old button gets a failed click and can click again. Discord does not document this and risa does not check it, so do not rely on the refusal. A view many people click at once fits InStore better: its custom_ids hold a key instead of the state, so they change only when a bound argument does.

Attributes:

  • codec (Codec) –

    How the state is written into custom_ids. risa.codecs.BASE85 by default; BASE32768 and URO14 from the [radixly] extra carry more than twice as much.

items.title: InStore
items.text:
InStore(ttl: float | None, store: str = DEFAULT_STORE, adopt: bool = False)

Bases: Struct

Keep a view's durable state in a store, under a key the message carries.

The components carry only a random key, and the state is one record in the client's store of the name store. It has no size bound, every process of a bot shares it through a distributed store, and it expires.

Attributes:

  • ttl (float | None) –

    Seconds an untouched record lives. Every click restarts the clock, so only abandoned views expire. None keeps records forever, including the ones a deleted message or a failed send leaves behind. There is no default, since no lifetime suits both a confirmation dialog and a role menu.

  • store (str) –

    Which of the client's stores holds the state: "default" for the client's store=, or a key of its stores=.

  • adopt (bool) –

    Take over the messages the view sent while it kept its state in the message. It needs the same version, and durable fields that can still read the old state. The first click on such a message moves its state into a record, which lives ttl like any other, and every later click on the message reads the record. Once the record has expired, the next click takes the state over again if the message still holds it. A message nobody clicks keeps its state. Without adopt, a click on a message nobody took over goes to on_outdated.

items.text:
PostgresStore(
    pool: Pool,
    *,
    table: str = DEFAULT_TABLE,
    lease: float = DEFAULT_LEASE,
    max_hold: float = DEFAULT_MAX_HOLD,
)

Bases: Store

A store on PostgreSQL, through an asyncpg pool.

An entry is a row of table. lock() takes a lease on a row of {table}_lease and renews it while held, so clicks on one view queue up across every process that shares the database. The store creates both tables on first use if they are missing, and deletes expired rows itself: on its first write, then on every hundredth.

    The pool the bot owns. The store borrows a connection for each statement and never opens or closes the pool.

  • lease (float, default: DEFAULT_LEASE ) –

    Seconds a lock's lease lasts. It is renewed every third of that while held, and a crashed holder blocks its view for at most this long.

  • max_hold (float, default: DEFAULT_MAX_HOLD ) –

    Seconds after which a held lock is no longer renewed, so a stuck handler cannot block its view for good.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    If table is not a plain lowercase identifier, lease is not positive, or max_hold is shorter than lease.

items.title: put_if_version async
items.text:
put_if_version(
    key: str, value: bytes, *, expected: int, ttl: float | None
) -> int | None

Write value under key only if the entry is still at version expected.

The compare and the write are one atomic step: of several writers expecting the same version, exactly one succeeds. ttl works as in put.

Parameters:

  • key (str) –

    The entry's key, as for get_versioned.

  • value (bytes) –

    The bytes to keep if the write goes through.

  • expected (int) –

    A version from get_versioned, or returned by an earlier put_if_version. The write goes through only while the entry is still at exactly that version. Versions compare only within one entry's life: a store may restart them once the entry is deleted or has expired.

  • ttl (float | None) –

    Seconds the entry lives from this write, as in put. None gives it no expiry.

Returns:

  • int | None –

    The entry's new version, or None if the entry is missing, expired, or at a different version, in which case nothing was written.

items.title: verify_store async
items.text:
verify_store(store: Store) -> None

Check that store behaves the way risa relies on.

Seventeen checks cover round trips, versions, the compare-and-set, expiry, touch and the lock. They run concurrently, each on its own random key under risa:conformance:, and each deletes what it wrote. Run it against a real instance of the backend, from a test or a script; it needs no test framework.

Parameters:

    The store to check, connected to a real instance of its backend.

    If any check fails. It lists every failure, not just the first.

items.text: A view is a whole message. You describe it once in render(), and risa turns it into the components Discord draws.

items.title: A view with no fields
items.text:
The counter in Your first view kept a number. This welcome message has no fields, so it has nothing to remember. It draws a box with two lines of text and a button, and the button answers with a message only the person who clicked can see.

@risa.register(name="welcome")
class Welcome(risa.View):
    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay("## Welcome to the server"),
            ui.TextDisplay("Read the rules, then say hello in **#general**."),
            ui.Row(ui.Button(self.rules, label="Show the rules")),
            accent_color=0xF680A1,
        )

    @risa.handler

items.title: From render() to Discord
items.text:
render() returns one component or a sequence of them, and Discord draws them in that order.

In render() In Discord ui.Container(...) A box around the components inside it, like an embed accent_color=0xF680A1 The colored bar down the left side of the box ui.TextDisplay("...") Text, in Discord's markdown ui.Row(...) A row of buttons, or one select menu ui.Button(self.rules, label="...") A button, and self.rules is the handler its clicks run

Selects, sections, galleries shows the other components.

items.title: A view is the whole message
items.text: A container or a text display makes the message a Components V2 message, and Discord's documentation says such a message has no content and no embeds. Text goes in ui.TextDisplay, so render() draws everything the message shows.

items.title: Register a view
items.text:
@risa.register makes the class a view and gives it a name. A click finds its view by that name, so keep the name once messages are out. client.add_view tells a client to answer for the view, once at startup.

client = risa.client_from_app(bot)
client.add_view(Welcome)

Without add_view the message still sends, but its clicks fail in Discord, and client.build logs a warning once. A client made with risa.client_from_app(bot, use_global=True) needs no add_view: it answers every view whose module has been imported.

items.title: Send it
items.text:
client.build renders a view and returns the result, ready to send. How you send it depends on where your code runs:

Your code runs in You send with An event, such as a new message await rendered.send_to(bot.rest, event.channel_id) A lightbulb command or a risa handler await ctx.respond(**rendered) A raw hikari interaction with no answer yet, such as a slash command await rendered.respond_to(bot.rest, interaction)

Leave content out of a call that spreads a Components V2 view. Rows alone are the one exception.

The example uses the first row: writing !welcome in a server channel posts the message. As with !counter in Your first view, the bot needs Message Content Intent turned on in the Developer Portal.

@bot.listen()
async def on_message(event: hikari.GuildMessageCreateEvent) -> None:
    if event.content == "!welcome":
        rendered = await client.build(Welcome())
        await rendered.send_to(bot.rest, event.channel_id)

items.title: Buttons that remember
items.text: A view's fields last from click to click and across restarts, and you store none of them. They travel in the message.

items.title: Fields are the state
items.text:
Every annotated field is saved. A new view starts from the defaults.

@risa.register(name="scoreboard")
class Scoreboard(risa.View):
    home: int = 0
    away: int = 0

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"## Home {self.home} : {self.away} Away"),
            ui.Row(
                ui.Button(self.score_home, label="Home +1"),
                ui.Button(self.score_away, label="Away +1"),
            ),
        )

To start somewhere else, pass values, as this preview does: client.build(Scoreboard(home=3, away=1)).

Each handler sees all the fields, whichever button was clicked, and ctx.rerender() draws the message from the new values.

    self.home += 1
    await ctx.rerender()

@risa.handler

    self.away += 1
    await ctx.rerender()

items.title: What a click goes through
items.text:
No view object waits in your bot between clicks. risa builds one for each click and fills it with the state from the message.

The state comes from the message and the class from add_view, which your code calls at every start, so a restart changes nothing.

Try it.

Stop the bot between two clicks on Home +1. A click while it is down fails in Discord, and the next click after the restart carries on from the old score.

items.title: Where the state sits
items.text:
risa writes the state into the hidden id of a button, its custom_id. Discord stores these ids with the message and sends them back with every click. These are the scoreboard's real ids, before and after a click on Home +1:

The state fits on Home +1, so Away +1 holds only its route. A click on Away +1 still finds the score, because Discord delivers the whole message with the click. State that does not fit on one button spreads over the others.

A click changes only the id that holds the state. Someone whose client still shows the old Home +1 gets a failed click and can click again.

The score is not secret.

Anyone who can see the message can read what the buttons hold, so keep secrets somewhere else.

items.title: What a field can hold
items.text:
A view is a msgspec.Struct, and a field can be anything msgspec encodes: numbers, strings, enums, lists, dicts, other Structs. It all has to fit in the message, which has room for about 60 bytes on one button and about 70 more for each further one, with the default codec. Where state lives shows what you can do when a view needs more.

For what should be read fresh instead of saved, such as a database row, mark the field risa.Prop[T] and fill it in load(), as Fresh data shows.

items.title: Handlers and arguments
items.text: One handler can serve many buttons, and each button can carry what it stands for.

items.title: An argument per button
items.text:
A ticket has a priority, and you want one button for each value, all running one handler. An enum.Enum holds the values.

class Priority(enum.Enum):
    LOW = 1
    NORMAL = 2
    URGENT = 3

risa.bind puts a value on a button, so render() binds one priority to each button it draws.

@risa.register(name="ticket")
class Ticket(risa.View):
    priority: Priority = Priority.NORMAL

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        buttons = [
            ui.Button(
                risa.bind(self.pick, priority),
                label=priority.name.title(),
                disabled=priority is self.priority,
            )
            for priority in Priority
        ]
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"Priority: **{self.priority.name.lower()}**"),
            ui.Row(*buttons),
        )

The handler receives the value as a parameter after ctx.

@risa.handler
async def pick(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext, priority: Priority) -> None:
    self.priority = priority
    await ctx.rerender()

Use a field for what changes while the view lives, and an argument for what a button stands for.

items.title: Where the argument sits
items.text: An argument travels in the button's custom_id, behind the route and any state, so risa's messages call it a wire argument. These are the ticket's real ids:

items.title: What can be an argument
items.text:
Arguments come right after ctx and are positional. They are annotated bool, int, str, hikari.Snowflake or an enum.Enum of int or str values. Every parameter after them without a default is filled in by dependency injection through linkd, as Dependency injection shows.

An argument takes room on its button, out of what the button can hold of the state. With the default codec, a button with no state holds a str of up to 68 ASCII characters, and a longer one makes client.build raise. Another codec fits more.

Used bare, @risa.handler takes the defaults. With options, it takes keywords, as in @risa.handler(handler_id="pick", version=2).

items.title: Selects, sections, galleries
items.text: A message can hold more than text and buttons: menus to pick from, an image or a button beside the text, galleries and files. Each is one more component for render() to return, and risa.ui.nodes lists them all with their options.

items.title: Picking from a list
items.text:
A ui.TextSelect fills a ui.Row by itself. ui.SelectOption("Ramen", "ramen") shows Ramen and hands you ramen, and without the second argument the value is the label.

@risa.register(name="lunch")
class Lunch(risa.View):
    choice: str = "not decided"

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:

            ui.TextDisplay(f"Lunch today: **{self.choice}**"),

                ui.TextSelect(
                    self.pick,
                    ui.SelectOption("Ramen", "ramen"),
                    ui.SelectOption("Curry", "curry"),
                    placeholder="Pick one",
                ),
            ),
        )

A pick routes to a handler as a click does, and ctx.values holds the value of each option the user picked. A menu takes one pick by default, and min_values and max_values change that.

    self.choice = ctx.values[0]
    await ctx.rerender()

items.title: Picking a user, a role or a channel
items.text:
Four more menus list what Discord already knows, so they take no options.

@risa.register(name="reviewer")
class Reviewer(risa.View):
    reviewer: str = "nobody"

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"Reviewer: **{self.reviewer}**"),
            ui.Row(ui.UserSelect(self.pick, placeholder="Pick a reviewer")),

ctx.values holds the ids of the picks, as strings, and ctx.resolved holds the objects, keyed by hikari.Snowflake. ctx.resolved can be None, so the handler checks it first.

@risa.handler
async def pick(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
    resolved = ctx.resolved
    if resolved is not None:
        user_id = hikari.Snowflake(ctx.values[0])
        self.reviewer = resolved.users[user_id].username
    await ctx.rerender()

items.text:
A ui.Section draws text with one accessory beside it: a thumbnail, a button or a link.

@risa.register(name="release")
class Release(risa.View):
    likes: int = 0

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:

        like = ui.Button(self.like, label="Like")

A ui.Button as an accessory routes like any other button, and it holds the state as one in a row would.

@risa.handler
async def like(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
    self.likes += 1
    await ctx.rerender()

ui.LinkButton opens a URL, and ui.PremiumButton(sku_id) offers one of your app's SKUs for purchase. Discord's documentation says neither sends your bot an interaction and neither can have a custom_id, so they take no handler and cannot hold state.

items.title: Answering in time
items.text: Discord gives a click three seconds. This chapter shows each way to answer, and what to do when the work takes longer.

items.title: The clock
items.text:
Discord's documentation asks for a first answer within 3 seconds of the click. Later answers go through a token that comes with the click, separate from your bot's token, and it stays valid for 15 minutes.

  1. 0 sThe clickThe clock starts.
  2. 2 sAuto-deferAnswers for a slow handler, if turned on.
  3. 3 sThe deadlineWith no answer, the click fails.
  4. 15 minThe token endsCalls through it stop working.

Auto-defer acknowledges the click in the handler's place. An acknowledgement counts as the first answer, so the click does not fail at 3 seconds, and the real answer can come later. The 2 seconds are the client's auto_defer_delay.

items.title: Which message
items.text:
Four calls answer a click, and they differ in which message they touch.

Call What it does AutoDefer for a slow handler ctx.rerender() Redraws the clicked message UPDATE ctx.edit(layout) Replaces the clicked message UPDATE ctx.replace(view) Turns the clicked message into another view UPDATE ctx.respond(...) Sends a new message THINKING or THINKING_EPHEMERAL

On a view with no slow handlers, a fast handler needs no auto-defer, because each of these calls is an answer in itself. AutoDefer.OFF is the default. Under THINKING, a slow rerender() edits the clicked message and leaves the thinking message with nothing to answer it, so a handler that redraws belongs with UPDATE.

items.title: A slow handler
items.text:
This report takes five seconds to build, so refresh and export need an auto-defer, and close needs one so that it is not stuck behind them.

@risa.register(name="report")
class Report(risa.View):
    rows: int = 0

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"Rows in the report: **{self.rows}**"),
            ui.Row(
                ui.Button(self.refresh, label="Refresh"),
                ui.Button(self.export, label="Export"),
                ui.Button(self.close, label="Close"),
            ),
        )

refresh redraws its own message. UPDATE acknowledges the click at 2 seconds with no sign the user can see, and ctx.rerender() edits the message when the report is ready.

@risa.handler(defer=risa.AutoDefer.UPDATE)
async def refresh(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
    self.rows = await build_report()
    await ctx.rerender()

export answers with a new message that only the person who clicked can see. THINKING_EPHEMERAL shows Discord's "thinking..." message at 2 seconds, and ctx.respond takes its place.

@risa.handler(defer=risa.AutoDefer.THINKING_EPHEMERAL)
async def export(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
    rows = await build_report()
    await ctx.respond(f"Exported {rows} rows.", ephemeral=True)

Keep ephemeral=True on the respond: a handler that finishes inside the 2 seconds answers through that call, with no thinking message before it.

close replaces the message with a layout render() does not draw, so the view ends here. Clicks on one message run one at a time, so a click on Close while refresh runs waits for it. UPDATE answers that click at 2 seconds, and the edit follows when its turn comes.

@risa.handler(defer=risa.AutoDefer.UPDATE)
async def close(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
    await ctx.edit(ui.TextDisplay(f"Closed with {self.rows} rows."))

items.title: By hand
items.text:
You can also acknowledge a click yourself, as ReportByHand in the full file does. ctx.defer() does it silently and right away, and ctx.defer(thinking=True, ephemeral=True) shows the thinking message.

@risa.handler
async def refresh(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
    await ctx.defer()
    self.rows = await build_report()
    await ctx.rerender()

defer() raises AlreadyRespondedError if the click already has its answer. It also runs only when the handler's turn comes, so a click waiting behind a slow handler on the same message can miss the 3 seconds. Auto-defer's timer starts before that wait, so use it on a view with slow handlers.

ctx.acknowledge() takes the same options and does nothing if the click already has its answer. It suits a handler with one branch that answers and one that does not.

@risa.handler
async def publish(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
    if self.rows == 0:
        await ctx.respond("There is nothing to publish.", ephemeral=True)
    else:
        await send_to_team(self.rows)
    await ctx.acknowledge()

items.title: Where to set it
items.text:
The handlers above set it for themselves. A view and the client take it too.

Set it on With It applies to A handler @risa.handler(defer=...) That handler A view @risa.register(defer=...) Its handlers with no setting of their own The client client_from_app(auto_defer=...) Handlers with neither setting

The most specific setting wins, so defer=risa.AutoDefer.OFF on a handler turns auto-defer off for it.

items.title: A handler that answers nothing
When something fails
items.text:
A failure can still get an answer. client.error_handler registers a function that risa calls when a click fails. This view asks a weather service that is down, and its Next city has a bug:

FORECASTS = {"Berlin": "Sunny, 18 °C"}


class ForecastUnavailableError(Exception):
    """The weather service did not answer."""


async def fetch_forecast(city: str) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    raise ForecastUnavailableError(city)


@risa.register(name="forecast")
class Forecast(risa.View):
    city: str = "Berlin"
    text: risa.Prop[str] = ""

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"**{self.city}**: {self.text or FORECASTS[self.city]}"),
            ui.Row(
                ui.Button(self.refresh, label="Refresh"),
                ui.Button(self.next_city, label="Next city"),
            ),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def refresh(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        self.text = await fetch_forecast(self.city)
        await ctx.rerender()

    @risa.handler
    async def next_city(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        self.city = "Paris"
        await ctx.rerender()

This error handler answers the failure the bot expects:

async def forecast_unavailable(failure: risa.ClickFailure) -> bool:
    if not isinstance(failure.error, ForecastUnavailableError):
        return False
    await failure.ctx.respond(
        "The weather service is not answering. Try again in a minute.",
        ephemeral=True,
    )
    return True

It gets a ClickFailure: failure.ctx to answer through, failure.error with the exception, and failure.stage with where it was raised. It returns True once it has dealt with the failure, and risa logs nothing more. With False it passes the failure on.

stage What failed HANDLER The handler LOAD load(), so the handler never ran ON_OUTDATED, ON_STATE_MISSING That hook STATE Reaching the view's state, before any of your code ran: the store failed or is missing, its lock timed out, or a codec's extra is not installed

A failure after the handler, such as saving the view when the handler returns, stays a log line.

Several error handlers run highest priority first, and in the order you registered them within one priority, until one returns True. If none does, risa logs the failure as it would without them. A last one that answers every failure and returns False tells the person something went wrong and still leaves the failure in your log:

async def something_went_wrong(failure: risa.ClickFailure) -> bool:
    await failure.ctx.respond("Something went wrong.", ephemeral=True)
    return False

def add_error_handlers(client: risa.Client) -> None:
    client.error_handler(forecast_unavailable, priority=1)
    client.error_handler(something_went_wrong, priority=-1)

@client.error_handler and @client.error_handler(priority=1) work as decorators too.

  • The view is gone. failure.ctx has no view state, as in on_outdated: respond, an edit with nothing to click and replace work, and on a view with fields rerender() raises NoViewError, so a half-changed view is never saved.
  • Three seconds. An error handler runs without auto-defer, and the three seconds count from the click. A failure that comes late, such as a lock that took ten seconds, leaves it no time unless auto-defer answered first.
  • What was sent before. respond continues it, as it would in the handler: after an answer it sends a follow-up, and after a thinking message it replaces that.
  • Injection. Its parameters after failure are injected, as a handler's are.
  • One that raises is logged and counts as False.

items.title: Dependency injection
items.text: A handler often needs something it doesn't make itself, such as your database. Register that thing once, name it as a parameter, and risa passes it in on every click.

items.title: What it is
items.text:
A dependency is anything your code needs but doesn't make itself: a database, an HTTP session, your config. A function can get one in two ways. It can open the thing itself:

async def price_of(item: str) -> int:
    database = await connect("postgres://localhost/shop")
    return await database.price(item)

That opens a new connection on every call, and each function that needs the database has to know how to open it. Or the function can name what it needs and leave the rest to whoever calls it:

async def price_of(item: str, database: Database) -> int:
    return await database.price(item)

This is dependency injection: the function says what it needs, and its caller passes it in. Every call can share one database, and only one place in your bot knows how to open it.

A handler works the same way, except that you never call it. A click comes in, and risa calls it. So you tell risa at startup what to pass, and the handler names what it wants. risa does this through linkd, the library lightbulb uses as well.

  1. 1You register itAt startup, you tell risa which object a Prices parameter gets.
  2. 2The handler names itIt takes a parameter, prices: Prices.
  3. 3risa passes it inOn each click, risa calls the handler with that object.

A view's field can't hold your database: fields get saved from click to click, and @risa.register raises ViewDeclarationError on a type it can't save. A global variable can, until you have something that opens only once the bot is running, such as a connection pool. The global stays empty until then, and each handler has to check it.

items.title: Register it
items.text:
This shop shows a price when someone clicks an item. Prices stands in for your database, and you can find it in the full file.

main() calls this once, before the bot starts:

def add_dependencies(client: risa.Client) -> None:
    registry = client.di.registry_for(risa.Contexts.DEFAULT)
    registry.register_value(Prices, Prices())

register_value(Prices, Prices()) says that a parameter annotated Prices gets this one object. How it works explains the line above it.

items.title: Name it as a parameter
items.text:
A click on an item runs show, which names what it needs.

@risa.handler
async def show(
    self,
    ctx: risa.ComponentContext,
    item: str,
    prices: Prices,
    client: risa.Client,
) -> None:
    offer = Offer(item=item, price=await prices.of(item))
    await ctx.respond(**await client.build(offer), ephemeral=True)
Parameter Filled by ctx risa, by position item: str The wire argument bound to the button prices: Prices, client: risa.Client Injection, going by the annotation, so any name will do

risa tells them apart by type. str is a type an argument can have, so item comes from the button. Prices is not, so prices is injected.

If nothing is registered for a parameter, the handler does not run: risa logs linkd's DependencyNotSatisfiableException, and the click fails in Discord.

items.title: Build another view
items.text:
show also names client, which you never registered, because risa registers it for you. A handler needs it for client.build, since the client is a local variable of main(). show builds an Offer and sends that as its answer. This is the other view, and main() adds both to the client.

@risa.register(name="offer")
class Offer(risa.View):
    item: str
    price: int

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"{self.item.title()}: {self.price} coins"),
            ui.Row(ui.Button(self.buy, label="Buy")),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def buy(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        await ctx.edit(ui.TextDisplay(f"You bought the {self.item}."))

That covers most bots. The rest of this page explains how injection works and what else it can do.

items.title: What risa registers
items.text:
risa registers these itself, so you can name them in any handler without registering anything.

For the whole run What it gets risa.Client The risa client, for client.build. risa.GatewayEnabledClient is not registered, so annotate it this way hikari.api.RESTClient The bot's REST client, for calling Discord beyond the answer to this click hikari.GatewayBot On a gateway bot, the bot, with its cache in bot.cache hikari.api.EventManager On a gateway bot, its event manager hikari.RESTBot On a REST bot, the bot hikari.api.InteractionServer On a REST bot, its interaction server For each click What it gets risa.ComponentContext The click, the same object as ctx. A factory or a function further down uses this to reach it hikari.ComponentInteraction The interaction behind the click, the same object as ctx.interaction

This handler uses the REST client to post in a log channel as well as answering the click:

@risa.handler
async def report(
    self,
    ctx: risa.ComponentContext,
    rest: hikari.api.RESTClient,
) -> None:
    await rest.create_message(_LOG_CHANNEL, f"{ctx.user.username} reported a problem.")
    await ctx.respond("Thanks, we'll take a look.", ephemeral=True)

items.title: How it works
items.text:
Three things work together.

Term What it is Context A lifetime with a name. risa.Contexts.DEFAULT lasts for the bot's whole run, and risa.Contexts.COMPONENT lasts for one click Registry The list of what a context can provide and how to make it. register_value adds to this list Container A box of live objects, made from a registry while its context is open. It makes each object the first time something asks for it, keeps it, and tears it down when the box closes

So client.di.registry_for(risa.Contexts.DEFAULT) reads as "the list for the whole run", and client.di is linkd's manager, which holds every list and box. There is one more context, risa.Contexts.MODAL, which waits for modals.

The boxes sit one inside the other. The objects below are the ones from the shop and the stall further down.

DEFAULT one container, open for the bot's whole run

risa.Client hikari.api.RESTClient Prices Database

COMPONENT a new container for each click

risa.ComponentContext hikari.ComponentInteraction Wallet

A handler runs here. It looks in this box first, then in the one around it.

  1. 1The clickrisa opens a COMPONENT container and puts ctx and the interaction in it.
  2. 2load() and the handlerFor each parameter, the container hands over what it holds, or makes it.
  3. 3The end of the clickThe container closes and tears down what it made.
  4. 4The next clickIt gets a new container. The DEFAULT one stays open.

Two rules follow from this:

  • A container only looks outward. A dependency in DEFAULT can't name one in COMPONENT, and a click that needs it fails with DependencyNotSatisfiableException.
  • A registry freezes while a container made from it is open. The DEFAULT container opens at the first click or load() and stays open, so a later register_value raises linkd's RegistryFrozenException. Register before the bot starts.

items.title: Values and factories
items.text:
register_value takes an object you already have. register_factory takes a function, and the container calls it the first time something names the type. Use it for what has to open inside the running event loop, such as a connection pool.

async def open_database(config: Config) -> Database:
    return await Database.connect(config.database_url)


def add_database(client: risa.Client) -> None:
    registry = client.di.registry_for(risa.Contexts.DEFAULT)
    registry.register_value(Config, Config())
    registry.register_factory(Database, open_database, teardown=Database.close)

A factory can be async, and its parameters are injected too, so open_database names Config and gets it from the same registry. If a factory raises, the handler does not run: risa logs DependencyNotSatisfiableException, and the click fails. Cleanup covers teardown.

items.title: A dependency for each click
items.text:
A wallet belongs to whoever clicked, so it can't exist before the click. Register it in COMPONENT, and each click gets its own.

async def open_wallet(ctx: risa.ComponentContext, database: Database) -> Wallet:
    coins = await database.coins_of(ctx.user.id)
    return Wallet(database, ctx.user.id, coins)


def add_wallet(client: risa.Client) -> None:
    registry = client.di.registry_for(risa.Contexts.COMPONENT)
    registry.register_factory(Wallet, open_wallet)

open_wallet names the click, which risa puts in the COMPONENT container, and Database, which the container finds in the DEFAULT one around it. A handler names Wallet like anything else.

@risa.handler
async def buy(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext, wallet: Wallet) -> None:
    if wallet.coins < self.price:
        await ctx.respond("You can't afford that.", ephemeral=True)
        return
    await wallet.pay(self.price)
    await ctx.respond(f"You have {wallet.coins} coins left.", ephemeral=True)

The container makes a wallet at most once per click, so load() and the handler of one click share it, and a handler that doesn't name it never opens one.

client.build runs load() in DEFAULT alone, even inside a handler. A load() that names Wallet makes it raise DependencyNotSatisfiableException, and one that names Wallet | None gets None there.

Full file 
"""A stall whose wallets open for each click, from a database that opens once."""

from __future__ import annotations

import os

import hikari

import risa
from risa import ui


class Config:
    database_url = "postgres://localhost/shop"


class Database:
    def __init__(self, url: str) -> None:
        self.url = url
        self.coins: dict[hikari.Snowflake, int] = {}

    @classmethod
    async def connect(cls, url: str) -> Database:
        return cls(url)

    async def close(self) -> None:
        self.coins.clear()

    async def coins_of(self, user: hikari.Snowflake) -> int:
        return self.coins.get(user, 10)

    async def set_coins(self, user: hikari.Snowflake, coins: int) -> None:
        self.coins[user] = coins


class Wallet:
    def __init__(self, database: Database, user: hikari.Snowflake, coins: int) -> None:
        self.database = database
        self.user = user
        self.coins = coins

    async def pay(self, price: int) -> None:
        self.coins -= price
        await self.database.set_coins(self.user, self.coins)


async def open_database(config: Config) -> Database:
    return await Database.connect(config.database_url)


def add_database(client: risa.Client) -> None:
    registry = client.di.registry_for(risa.Contexts.DEFAULT)
    registry.register_value(Config, Config())
    registry.register_factory(Database, open_database, teardown=Database.close)


async def open_wallet(ctx: risa.ComponentContext, database: Database) -> Wallet:
    coins = await database.coins_of(ctx.user.id)
    return Wallet(database, ctx.user.id, coins)


def add_wallet(client: risa.Client) -> None:
    registry = client.di.registry_for(risa.Contexts.COMPONENT)
    registry.register_factory(Wallet, open_wallet)


@risa.register(name="stall")
class Stall(risa.View):
    price: int = 3

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"An apple costs {self.price} coins."),
            ui.Row(ui.Button(self.buy, label="Buy")),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def buy(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext, wallet: Wallet) -> None:
        if wallet.coins < self.price:
            await ctx.respond("You can't afford that.", ephemeral=True)
            return
        await wallet.pay(self.price)
        await ctx.respond(f"You have {wallet.coins} coins left.", ephemeral=True)


def main() -> None:
    bot = hikari.GatewayBot(
        os.environ["DISCORD_TOKEN"],
        intents=hikari.Intents.ALL_UNPRIVILEGED | hikari.Intents.MESSAGE_CONTENT,
    )
    client = risa.client_from_app(bot)
    add_database(client)
    add_wallet(client)
    client.add_view(Stall)

    @bot.listen()
    async def on_message(event: hikari.GuildMessageCreateEvent) -> None:
        if event.content == "!stall":
            rendered = await client.build(Stall())
            await rendered.send_to(bot.rest, event.channel_id)

    @bot.listen()
    async def on_stopping(_: hikari.StoppingEvent) -> None:
        await client.di.close()


    bot.run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

items.title: Overriding a dependency
items.text: Register a type in COMPONENT that DEFAULT has too, and a click gets the COMPONENT one. A dependency made in DEFAULT keeps using the DEFAULT one, because a container only looks outward.

items.title: Adding to an open container
items.text:
A frozen registry takes nothing new, but an open container does. container.add_value and container.add_factory add to that one container, and what they add goes when it closes. linkd calls these ephemeral dependencies, and risa adds ctx this way. A handler reaches its container by naming it, and a function further down then gets what it added.

@risa.handler
async def flag(
    self,
    ctx: risa.ComponentContext,
    container: risa.ComponentContainer,
) -> None:
    container.add_value(Reason, Reason(f"Flagged by {ctx.user.username}."))
    await record()
    await ctx.respond("Flagged.", ephemeral=True)
Container What it gets risa.ComponentContainer The click's container linkd.RootContainer The DEFAULT container linkd.Container The innermost open container, which in a handler is the click's

items.title: Two of one type
items.text:
A type has one registration. For two databases, make a class for each, and name those.

class Primary(Database):
    pass


class Replica(Database):
    pass


def add_databases(client: risa.Client) -> None:
    registry = client.di.registry_for(risa.Contexts.DEFAULT)
    registry.register_value(Primary, Primary("primary"))
    registry.register_value(Replica, Replica("replica"))

@risa.handler
async def vote(
    self,
    ctx: risa.ComponentContext,
    primary: Primary,
    replica: Replica,
) -> None:
    await primary.add_vote(ctx.user.id)
    total = await replica.count_votes()
    await ctx.respond(f"{total} votes so far.", ephemeral=True)

If a library makes the object for you, so that a subclass won't do, wrap it in a small class of your own. linkd also accepts a typing.NewType as the type, but pyright rejects it in register_value.

items.title: Optional dependencies
items.text:
Annotate a parameter Metrics | None, and it gets None when nothing is registered.

@risa.handler
async def like(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext, metrics: Metrics | None) -> None:
    if metrics is not None:
        metrics.count("likes")
    await ctx.respond("Thanks!", ephemeral=True)

A union falls back the same way: Memory | Disk gets the first one registered. linkd.Try[Memory] | Disk also falls back when making Memory fails, where a plain union would fail the click.

items.title: Where injection works
items.text:
Handlers, load(), on_state_missing, on_outdated, error handlers and factories have it without a decorator. For a function of your own, add @linkd.inject. render() takes no injected parameters, so load() reads what it draws.

A parameter is injected if it has an annotation and either no default or the default risa.INJECTED. Any other default stays as it is. *args, **kwargs and positional-only parameters are left alone. A parameter with no annotation gets nothing, so the click fails with a TypeError.

risa.INJECTED tells your type checker that nobody has to pass the parameter. on_outdated, on_state_missing and a function of your own that you call with no arguments need it. In a handler it also marks a wire type as injected: limit: int = risa.INJECTED.

items.title: Injection context
items.text:
An injected function needs an open context when it runs. risa opens DEFAULT and COMPONENT around load(), the handler, the hooks and the error handlers of a click, and DEFAULT around the load() in client.build. A function called from inside those has them too, so you rarely need to think about this.

Anywhere else, such as in a hikari listener, open the context yourself, or the call raises DependencyNotSatisfiableException.

@linkd.inject
async def post_votes(
    rest: hikari.api.RESTClient = risa.INJECTED,
    replica: Replica = risa.INJECTED,
) -> None:
    total = await replica.count_votes()
    await rest.create_message(_LOG_CHANNEL, f"{total} votes so far.")


def post_on_start(bot: hikari.GatewayBot, client: risa.Client) -> None:
    @bot.listen()
    async def on_started(_: hikari.StartedEvent) -> None:
        async with client.di.enter_context(risa.Contexts.DEFAULT):
            await post_votes()

items.title: Cleanup
items.text:
Give a dependency a teardown, a function that takes the dependency, as open_database above does with Database.close. It runs when the dependency's container closes, and only if the container made it.

A COMPONENT container closes at the end of each click, even if the handler raised. The DEFAULT container stays open until you close it, and risa never does, so call client.di.close() when the bot stops.

Gateway botREST bot 
@bot.listen()
async def on_stopping(_: hikari.StoppingEvent) -> None:
    await client.di.close()

async def close_dependencies(_: hikari.RESTBot) -> None:
    await client.di.close()

bot.add_shutdown_callback(close_dependencies)

With lightbulb, lightbulb_client.stop closes the shared manager, so bot.subscribe(hikari.StoppingEvent, lightbulb_client.stop) is enough.

items.title: Share one manager with lightbulb
items.text:
risa.client_from_lightbulb makes a client on lightbulb's manager, so what you register with lightbulb reaches your handlers too. lightbulb registers the hikari types above itself.

registry = lightbulb_client.di.registry_for(lightbulb.di.Contexts.DEFAULT)
registry.register_value(Prices, Prices())
risa_client = risa.client_from_lightbulb(lightbulb_client)
risa_client.add_view(Shop)
lightbulb_client.register(ShopCommand)

A command gets the risa client the same way:

class ShopCommand(
    lightbulb.SlashCommand,
    name="shop",
    description="Open the shop.",
):
    @lightbulb.invoke
    async def invoke(self, ctx: lightbulb.Context, client: risa.Client) -> None:
        await ctx.respond(**await client.build(Shop()))

risa.Contexts.DEFAULT and lightbulb's DEFAULT are the same context, linkd's root. A click opens risa's COMPONENT and a command opens lightbulb's COMMAND, and neither sees what the other registers.

items.title: Turning it off
items.text: Set the environment variable LINKD_DI_DISABLED to true to turn linkd off. risa passes ctx and the wire arguments itself, so a handler that takes only those keeps working. A handler that names anything else fails with a TypeError.

items.title: Types have to exist at runtime
items.text: linkd reads annotations while the bot runs, so a dependency's type has to be importable then. A type imported only under if typing.TYPE_CHECKING: makes @risa.register raise HandlerSignatureError for a handler, and NameError for a load() or a factory. Keep that import outside the block.

items.title: Fresh data with Prop and load()
items.text: Some things should be read fresh on every click instead of saved in the message, such as a database row. Mark them risa.Prop and fill them in load().

items.title: A leaderboard
items.text:
game is a field like any other, saved in the message. rows is a risa.Prop, and load() fills it. Scores stands in for your database, and you can find it in the full file.

@risa.register(name="leaderboard")
class Leaderboard(risa.View):
    game: str = "chess"
    rows: risa.Prop[list[str]] = msgspec.field(default_factory=list[str])

    async def load(self, scores: Scores) -> None:
        self.rows = await scores.top(self.game)

load() names Scores as a parameter, as a handler would, and main() registers it. Without that, client.build raises linkd's DependencyNotSatisfiableException. msgspec.field(default_factory=list[str]) gives each view a new empty list.

render() reads a prop as it reads a field. Each game's button runs switch, and _TOP at the top of the file holds each game's top players.

def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
    lines = [f"{n}. {name}" for n, name in enumerate(self.rows, start=1)]
    buttons = [
        ui.Button(
            risa.bind(self.switch, game),
            label=game.title(),
            disabled=game == self.game,
        )
        for game in _TOP
    ]
    return ui.Container(
        ui.TextDisplay(f"## Top players in {self.game}"),
        ui.TextDisplay("\n".join(lines)),
        ui.Row(*buttons, ui.Button(self.refresh, label="Refresh")),
    )

items.title: What a prop costs
items.text:
A prop takes no room in the message: nothing about rows goes into the buttons' ids, however many rows load() returns. It needs a default, because each click builds the view with its props at their defaults before load() runs, and without one @risa.register raises ViewDeclarationError.

A prop is never saved, so what a handler puts in one lasts for that click's rerender, and the next click starts from the default again.

items.title: When load() runs
items.text:
1. 1Fields returnFrom the message.
  2. 2load()Fills the props.
  3. 3The handlerChanges fields.
  4. 4rerender()Draws fields and props.

client.build runs it too, before render(), so the first message has its rows. On a click, refresh only rerenders, and the rows are new because load() has just read them.

@risa.handler
async def refresh(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
    await ctx.rerender()

load() runs inside the three seconds from Answering in time, and its time counts toward auto-defer's 2 seconds.

items.title: A handler that changes what load() reads
items.text:
load() runs before the handler, and not again.

A handler that sets self.game and calls ctx.rerender() draws the new heading over the old rows, because load() read them while game still held the old value.

Read them again in the handler. switch takes the game as a wire argument, as in Handlers and arguments, and after it scores, which risa injects as it does for load(). A handler's injected parameter needs no default.

@risa.handler
async def switch(
    self,
    ctx: risa.ComponentContext,
    game: str,
    scores: Scores,
) -> None:
    self.game = game
    self.rows = await scores.top(game)
    await ctx.rerender()

items.title: Where state lives
items.text: A view's state sits in its message until the message runs out of room. This chapter shows what you can do then, and how to choose between the message and a store.

items.title: What you can do
items.text:
Smallest step first. The last column counts for the poll below, which fits twelve voters as it is:

Step What you write Room for voters Read it fresh Mark the field risa.Prop[T] and fill it in load() from your database The field takes none Another codec state=risa.InMessage(codec=risa.codecs.BASE32768), with the radixly extra 33 voters, or 30 with URO14 A store state=risa.InStore(ttl=...), as Stores and TTL shows No size limit

A codec change leaves messages already sent working, since each id names its codec. A prop or a move to a store retires them: a click on one fails in Discord, unless a class at the old version answers it.

items.title: A poll that outgrows its message
items.text:
This poll counts the votes and keeps the id of everyone who voted, so that nobody votes twice.

@risa.register(name="poll")
class Poll(risa.View):
    question: str
    yes: int = 0
    no: int = 0
    voters: list[int] = msgspec.field(default_factory=list[int])

Yes and No each ask this method first, and it adds the voter's id to the list.

async def _first_vote(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> bool:
    if ctx.user.id in self.voters:
        await ctx.respond("You already voted.", ephemeral=True)
        return False
    self.voters.append(ctx.user.id)
    return True

items.title: The limit
items.text:
Two buttons hold 140 bytes, framing included, and each voter takes 9 of them. With the question and the counts, twelve voters fit:

The thirteenth does not. client.build raises StateOverflowError, and the error lists what each field takes:

A running poll gets this error from ctx.rerender() in the thirteenth voter's click. Nothing has been written yet, so the message keeps twelve votes. If the handler lets the error through, risa logs it and the click fails in Discord. This poll catches it and answers instead:

async def _save(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
    try:
        await ctx.rerender()
    except risa.StateOverflowError:
        await ctx.respond("This poll is full.", ephemeral=True)

self still holds the thirteenth vote. When the handler returns, risa tries to save it once more, finds that it still does not fit, and leaves it at a DEBUG line, since the handler has dealt with it. A handler that goes on to change the poll after the except saves that change together with the thirteenth vote, which does not fit either, so it takes the vote back first.

At twelve voters the state fills both buttons:

The voters are not secret.

render() shows only the totals, but the voters' ids travel in the pink part. Anyone who can see the message can read who voted.

Each vote also changes these ids. When tested, Discord refused a click on an old id, so of two people voting at the same moment, the second can get a failed click and has to click again.

items.title: Another codec
items.text:
A codec decides how risa writes a view's state into the ids of its buttons. Discord allows 100 characters per id, however many bytes each character takes, so a codec with more characters to choose from fits more into each one. The default, BASE85, uses 85 ASCII characters and writes 6.4 bits with each. BASE32768 chooses from 32,768 characters and writes 15. When tested, ids of 100 such characters came back from Discord byte for byte.

Codec Bits per character One button holds The poll fits A bound str, in ASCII characters BASE85 6.4 70 bytes 12 voters 68 BASE32768 15 165 bytes 33 voters 159 URO14 14 152 bytes 30 voters 147

The bytes include 9 of framing per view, so the default codec leaves about 60 for your state on one button, and about 70 for each further one. The last column is for a button with no state, as in What can be an argument.

To switch, install the radixly extra:

uvpip 
uv add "hikari-risa[radixly]"

pip install "hikari-risa[radixly]"

Then name the codec on the view with risa.InMessage. Nothing else in the view changes.

@risa.register(name="poll", state=risa.InMessage(codec=risa.codecs.BASE32768))
class Poll(risa.View):
    question: str
    yes: int = 0
    no: int = 0
    voters: list[int] = msgspec.field(default_factory=list[int])

Compare the ids with the ones above: the same twelve voters now fit on the first button, and the second has no state at all.

You don't raise version, and messages already sent keep working. Each id names its codec, so risa reads an old message in the codec it was written in, and writes it in the new one at its next rerender. A poll that was full gets its room with the next vote.

BASE32768 holds the most, so take it unless you have a reason not to. URO14 holds a little less and writes only characters from one CJK block. InMessage(codec=...) also takes a Codec of your own.

Keep these in mind:

  • There is still a limit. The 34th voter raises StateOverflowError, where a store has no limit.
  • The state stays readable. The ids look scrambled, but anyone can decode them, so a codec is no encryption.
  • Each vote still changes the ids, so two people voting at the same moment can still get a failed click.
  • The extra has to stay installed. Without radixly, @risa.register raises CodecUnavailableError on a view that names the codec. A click on a message written in it logs an error that names the extra, and the click fails.
  • A codec of your own has to stay registered. Once no view names it, call risa.codecs.register on it in every process that answers clicks. Otherwise risa takes its ids for another bot's and ignores them, so the click fails with no line in your log.
  • Going back can overflow. A message that holds more than the old codec fits fails at its next rerender with StateOverflowError.

A codec is only for the message. InStore has no codec, since its buttons hold a short key.

items.title: Message or store
items.text:
The message, risa.InMessage, is the default. It needs no infrastructure, and the state lives as long as the message does. Move to a store when the view needs one of these:

The view needs A store gives it Room No size limit A lifetime A ttl, where state in a message never expires Data not everyone should read Buttons that hold a random key, with the state out of sight Many people clicking at once Ids that change only with a bound argument, so a vote leaves them as they are

Where the bot runs counts too, as Several processes shows.

Full file 
"""A poll that records who voted, in the message, until the message runs out of room."""

from __future__ import annotations

import os

import hikari
import msgspec

import risa
from risa import ui


@risa.register(name="poll")
class Poll(risa.View):
    question: str
    yes: int = 0
    no: int = 0
    voters: list[int] = msgspec.field(default_factory=list[int])

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"## {self.question}"),
            ui.Row(
                ui.Button(self.vote_yes, label=f"Yes: {self.yes}"),
                ui.Button(self.vote_no, label=f"No: {self.no}"),
            ),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def vote_yes(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        if await self._first_vote(ctx):
            self.yes += 1
            await self._save(ctx)

    @risa.handler
    async def vote_no(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        if await self._first_vote(ctx):
            self.no += 1
            await self._save(ctx)

    async def _first_vote(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> bool:
        if ctx.user.id in self.voters:
            await ctx.respond("You already voted.", ephemeral=True)
            return False
        self.voters.append(ctx.user.id)
        return True

    async def _save(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        try:
            await ctx.rerender()
        except risa.StateOverflowError:
            await ctx.respond("This poll is full.", ephemeral=True)


def main() -> None:
    bot = hikari.GatewayBot(
        os.environ["DISCORD_TOKEN"],
        intents=hikari.Intents.ALL_UNPRIVILEGED | hikari.Intents.MESSAGE_CONTENT,
    )
    client = risa.client_from_app(bot)
    client.add_view(Poll)

    @bot.listen()
    async def on_message(event: hikari.GuildMessageCreateEvent) -> None:
        if event.content == "!poll":
            rendered = await client.build(Poll(question="Pizza on Friday?"))
            await rendered.send_to(bot.rest, event.channel_id)

    bot.run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

items.title: Stores and TTL
items.text: A store gives the poll room for every voter and a lifetime. This chapter moves the poll into one, first in memory and then in Redis.

items.title: Moving the poll
items.text:
risa.InStore on @risa.register moves the view, and it takes ttl, in seconds. The handlers stay as they were. Polls already sent cannot follow on their own, so version goes up, as Changing a view safely explains. To keep old polls working instead, leave version as it is and pass adopt=True: the first click on an old poll moves its votes into the store.

@risa.register(name="poll", version=2, state=risa.InStore(ttl=WEEK))
class Poll(risa.View):
    question: str
    yes: int = 0
    no: int = 0
    voters: list[int] = msgspec.field(default_factory=list[int])

The thirteen voters that raised an error now fit:

The buttons hold a random key to one record in the store, so the voters' ids stay out of the message, and a vote leaves the buttons' ids as they are:

items.title: MemoryStore
items.text:
A client gets its store from store=. risa.MemoryStore needs nothing installed.

client = risa.client_from_app(bot, store=risa.MemoryStore())
client.add_view(Poll)

It keeps the records in your bot's memory, and that has its price:

  • A restart loses every record, and a click on a poll sent before it runs on_state_missing.
  • Only the process that sent a poll holds its record, so a bot of several processes misses most clicks.
  • Past max_entries, 10,000 unless you pass another, each new record pushes out the one unused the longest.

That is fine while you try things out, and for a bot of one process whose polls may reset when it restarts. add_view warns you about it:

Once you choose it on purpose, risa.MemoryStore(warn=False) turns that warning off. The one at max_entries stays.

A bot with several stores passes stores={"votes": store}, and the view names one with risa.InStore(ttl=WEEK, store="votes").

add_view raises ViewDeclarationError at startup if the client has no store for the view. A client made with use_global=True skips add_view and finds out late: client.build raises, and a click on a poll already sent fails, with an ERROR in your log.

items.title: ttl
items.text:
ttl is how many seconds a record lives untouched. Every click restarts the clock, even one that changes nothing, so only a poll nobody clicks for a week expires. ttl=None keeps a record forever, including one that a deleted message, a view you ended or a failed send leaves behind.

The message stays as it is when the time runs out, and the next click runs on_state_missing.

@classmethod
async def on_state_missing(cls, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
    await ctx.edit(ui.TextDisplay("This poll has expired."))

Without this method the click fails in Discord, and risa logs a warning. ctx has no view here, so ctx.respond and a ctx.edit with nothing to click work, and ctx.rerender() raises NoViewError, as a ctx.edit with a button does.

items.title: Redis and PostgreSQL
items.text:
These two keep the state through a restart, and all processes of a bot can share them. Each lives in a module of its own and needs its extra.

Store Extra It takes risa.store.redis.RedisStore redis A redis.asyncio.Redis risa.store.postgres.PostgresStore postgres An asyncpg pool

The connection stays yours, so the bot closes it when it stops. An asyncpg pool opens inside the running event loop, so make the pool and the client in a hikari.StartingEvent listener.

connection = redis.asyncio.Redis(host="localhost")
client = risa.client_from_app(bot, store=RedisStore(connection))
client.add_view(Poll)

@bot.listen()
async def on_stopped(_: hikari.StoppedEvent) -> None:
    await connection.aclose()

Try it.

Vote, stop the bot and start it again. A second vote from you gets "You already voted.", because the record is still there.

Turn on AOF as well (appendonly yes, appendfsync everysec), because RDB snapshots alone lose recent votes in a crash.

PostgreSQL needs no cleanup job: PostgresStore creates its tables on first use and deletes expired rows itself.

items.title: Changing a view safely
items.text:
A message outlives the code that sent it: someone can click last month's poll on the code you released today. This chapter shows which changes break those old buttons, and every way to deal with one that does.

Before you release a change, look it up under What breaks. If it is free, release it. If it breaks old buttons, pick from What you can do, or from Changing a handler if only a handler changed.

items.title: Why an old button can break
items.text:
A button's custom_id stays as the old code wrote it until the message's next rerender. These are a poll's ids:

On a click, risa holds what the id says against the code running now, in this order:

  1. 1The viewIts name and version. With no class at that version, the click fails in Discord and none of your code runs.
  2. 2The handlerIts handler_id and version. With no such method, on_outdated runs.
  3. 3The argumentsTheir types, then their values. With other types, or an enum value that is gone, on_outdated runs.
  4. 4The stateThe fields that wrote it. If they no longer fit, on_outdated runs. If a store has lost the record, on_state_missing runs.

If all four pass, the handler runs: today's code on the old state.

items.title: Free changes
items.text:
Old buttons keep working through all of these:

You change What to know The code of render(), load(), a handler or a hook An old message keeps its look until its next rerender A button added to render(), or left out A button you left out stays on old messages until their next rerender, so keep its handler until then The Python name of the class or its module risa routes by name= A field added at the end, with a default It takes room in a message A field's default, or a default added to a field State that holds the field keeps its value, and state saved before the field existed gets the current default A risa.Prop, added, changed or removed Props are not saved A field from int to hikari.Snowflake Both are saved the same way A value added to a field's enum.Enum, or to a Literal of the same kinds of values risa compares only whether the values are int, str or None An enum member's name, if its value stays risa saves the value ttl An old record takes it at its next click, or None at its next save InMessage to InStore(adopt=True), with the same version An old message moves its state into the store at its next click The codec An old message takes it at its next rerender, as long as risa can still read the old one A handler's parameter names, its defer, or an injected parameter added See Changing a handler

Here is the most useful one. This poll gets a note under its question, in a field at the end of the class:

@risa.register(name="poll", version=2, state=risa.InStore(ttl=WEEK))
class Poll(risa.View):

    voters: list[int] = msgspec.field(default_factory=list[int])
    note: str = "One vote each."

            ui.Row(
                ui.Button(self.vote_yes, label=f"Yes: {self.yes}"),
                ui.Button(self.vote_no, label=f"No: {self.no}"),
            ),
        )

In a message the new field takes room too: with this note, the poll from Where state lives has room for ten voters, and one that already holds ten or more fails on its next vote.
