items.title: Breaking changes
items.text:
You change A click on an old message risa logs The view's version or name Fails in Discord DEBUG A field: removed, renamed, reordered or retyped on_outdated ERROR A field added anywhere but the end, or with no default on_outdated ERROR A field made a risa.Prop on_outdated ERROR A value removed from a field's enum.Enum or Literal, or changed on_outdated, only for messages that hold it WARNING A field's Literal gains a kind of value, or loses its last value of one on_outdated ERROR A field's nested struct changes on_outdated ERROR InMessage to InStore without adopt=True, or InStore to InMessage on_outdated ERROR Another store, or another key_prefix on_state_missing WARNING, or DEBUG once you override it Less room in a message: more state, or fewer buttons to hold it The handler runs, and rerender() raises StateOverflowError ERROR A method renamed or deleted, or its version raised with no method left at the old one on_outdated WARNING, or DEBUG once you override it A handler's arguments: added, removed or retyped on_outdated ERROR A codec old messages use: its extra removed, or your own no longer registered Fails in Discord ERROR for the extra, nothing for your own A bound enum member removed, or its value changed on_outdated WARNING An argument's default removed, from a button that left the argument out on_outdated ERROR

on_outdated and on_state_missing do nothing until you override them, so without that, a click that reaches them fails in Discord too.

An enum with a _missing_ method decides itself what a removed value becomes, in a field and in an argument. The handler then runs with the member it returns, and on_outdated stays out of it.

The ERROR lines on fields and arguments usually mean a forgotten version, and they tell you to raise it. hikari logs at INFO by default, so you see no line for a raised version until you turn DEBUG on.

items.title: What risa cannot see
items.text: risa compares names and types. If price: int held cents and now holds euros, every check passes, and your handler reads old cents as euros. An argument that keeps its type and changes its meaning is the same, and so are two enum members that swap their values. Raise the version yourself when a meaning changes.

items.title: In a message or in a store
items.text:
This chapter's rules hold for InMessage and InStore alike, and its poll sits in a store. These are the differences:

InMessage InStore New fields Take room, and a message that no longer fits fails at its next save No limit Fewer buttons Less room, with the same failure No effect, since each button holds the same key State that is gone Cannot happen, so on_state_missing never runs An expired record, another store or another key_prefix run on_state_missing What a retired message leaves behind Nothing Its record, until its ttl runs out, or for good under ttl=None A bound argument Shares its id with the state Shares its id with the key Free to change The codec ttl

items.title: What you can do
items.text:
Say the poll should take any options, not only yes and no. yes and no become one votes dict, and vote_yes and vote_no become one handler with an argument. The fields changed, so the view's version goes up to 3.

@risa.register(name="poll", version=3, state=risa.InStore(ttl=WEEK))
class Poll(risa.View):
    question: str
    votes: dict[str, int]
    voters: list[int] = msgspec.field(default_factory=list[int])
    note: str = "One vote each."

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        buttons = [
            ui.Button(
                risa.bind(self.vote, option),
                label=f"{option}: {count}",
            )
            for option, count in self.votes.items()
        ]
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"## {self.question}"),
            ui.TextDisplay(self.note),
            ui.Row(*buttons),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def vote(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext, option: str) -> None:
        if ctx.user.id in self.voters:
            await ctx.respond("You already voted.", ephemeral=True)
            return
        self.voters.append(ctx.user.id)
        self.votes[option] += 1
        await ctx.rerender()

Polls already sent stay at version 2. These are your options for them, and you can choose per old version:

Option A click on an old poll What stays in your code Make the change free Works The old fields or handlers, next to the new ones Let old buttons fail Fails in Discord Nothing Answer them all the same way Gets one reply A small class Close the old message Shows the final result, and the buttons go The old fields and a method per old button Keep the old version running Works as before The whole old class Upgrade the old message Turns the poll into version 3 The old fields, a method per old button, the conversion

items.title: Make the change free
items.text:
Many breaking changes have a free form that reaches the same goal:

Instead of Do this Renaming or retyping a field Keep it, add the new one at the end with a default, and read both Renaming a method Pin its handler_id Changing a handler's arguments Keep a method at the old version

For the poll, yes and no would stay behind the two old buttons, and a more: dict[str, int] at the end would hold the other options. Old polls keep working, and you carry both forms for as long as those polls matter.

items.title: Let old buttons fail
items.text:
Raise the version and do nothing else. A click on an old poll reaches no view, so it fails in Discord. on_outdated on the new class does not run, because that class answers only for version 3. For this poll in a store, that looks like this:

  1. MondayVersion 2 sends a pollIts buttons route to version 2 and hold the record's key.
  2. TuesdayYou release version 3New polls route to version 3. The old message stays as it was.
  3. WednesdaySomeone clicks the old pollThe click fails in Discord, unless a class at version 2 answers it.
  4. A week after the last click that read itThe record expiresThe message stays, and a later click finds no record.

This suits messages nobody comes back to.

items.title: Answer them all the same way
items.text:
A class at the old version needs no fields, no handlers and no state=. Every old button finds no handler there, so on_outdated answers it. Add the class to the client as well. This one answers the oldest polls, from version 1 in Where state lives:

@risa.register(name="poll", version=1)
class RetiredPoll(risa.View):
    @classmethod
    async def on_outdated(cls, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        await ctx.respond("This button no longer works.", ephemeral=True)

The old state is out of reach here. To replace the message, so nobody clicks it again, call ctx.edit(ui.TextDisplay("...")) instead.

Each old version needs a class of its own, and a base class can hold the answer once:

class Retired(risa.View):
    @classmethod
    async def on_outdated(cls, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        await ctx.respond("This button no longer works.", ephemeral=True)


@risa.register(name="poll", version=1)
class PollV1(Retired): ...

items.title: Upgrade the old message
items.text:
If the old state converts to the new, let the next click do it. These handlers build a version 3 poll from the version 2 state and count the vote. ctx.replace then turns the message into that poll.

@risa.register(name="poll", version=2, state=risa.InStore(ttl=WEEK))
class OldPoll(risa.View):
    question: str
    yes: int = 0
    no: int = 0
    voters: list[int] = msgspec.field(default_factory=list[int])
    note: str = ""

    @risa.handler
    async def vote_yes(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        await self._upgrade(ctx, "Yes")

    @risa.handler
    async def vote_no(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        await self._upgrade(ctx, "No")

    async def _upgrade(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext, option: str) -> None:
        poll = Poll(
            question=self.question,
            votes={"Yes": self.yes, "No": self.no},
            voters=self.voters,
            note=self.note,
        )
        if ctx.user.id not in poll.voters:
            poll.voters.append(ctx.user.id)
            poll.votes[option] += 1
        await ctx.replace(poll)
  • ctx.edit cannot do this. It takes only the buttons of the view that was clicked, and raises LayoutError for another's.
  • The old view stops here. Its state is not saved, and ctx.rerender() and ctx.edit() raise NoViewError.
  • The new state. In a store, ctx.replace writes a new record under a new key, and the old one expires with its ttl. In a message, it raises StateOverflowError if the new state does not fit the new buttons.
  • Messages nobody clicks. risa keeps no list of the messages it sent, so one that gets no click stays at version 2. It still needs this class when someone clicks it next.
  • Two clicks at once. Both start from the same old state, and the second replaces the first with only its own vote.

When the old state cannot convert, close the message instead. A count of votes cannot say who chose what, so a version that records it has nothing to fill it with.

items.title: Changing a handler
items.text:
A handler has a route of its own, so you can change one and leave the rest of the view working. A button holds three things about its handler:

The button holds Set by handler_id @risa.handler, the method's name by default version @risa.handler, 1 by default A fingerprint of the argument types The parameters after ctx that risa.bind fills

What stays outside these is free: the body, defer, a parameter's name, an injected parameter, a default added to an argument, int to hikari.Snowflake, and a member added to a bound enum.

items.title: Renaming a method
items.text:
Pin the old name as handler_id, and buttons already sent reach the method under its new name. This method used to be called vote:

@risa.handler(handler_id="vote")
async def vote_by_name(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext, option: str) -> None:
    await self._count(ctx, option)

With no pin, the route changes with the name, and old buttons go to on_outdated.

items.title: Changing its arguments
items.text:
An option's name travels on its button, and in this poll, in a store, it can be 54 ASCII characters long before client.build raises, and fewer of anything else, since a str takes its UTF-8 bytes. So the buttons should carry the option's position instead, and option: str becomes position: int. Old buttons still hold a str, so the new method gets a new version, and the method above stays at the old one.

@risa.handler(version=2)
async def vote(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext, position: int) -> None:
    await self._count(ctx, list(self.votes)[position])

render() binds self.vote, which is version 2:

def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
    buttons = [
        ui.Button(risa.bind(self.vote, position), label=f"{option}: {count}")
        for position, (option, count) in enumerate(self.votes.items())
    ]
    return ui.Container(
        ui.TextDisplay(f"## {self.question}"),
        ui.TextDisplay(self.note),
        ui.Row(*buttons),
    )

Button Holds Reaches Already sent vote, version 1, a str vote_by_name Drawn by render() vote, version 2, an int vote

vote_by_name ends in ctx.rerender(), which draws version 2 buttons, so an old poll moves over at its first click. Two methods with the same id and the same version raise DuplicateHandlerError at @risa.register.

If you change the arguments and keep the version, each old button goes to on_outdated with an ERROR line that names the fix.

items.title: Retiring a handler
items.text: Delete the method once no old button matters. Unlike a raised view version, this reaches the current class, so its on_outdated answers. To answer with what the view holds, keep the method and let its body say so, as the closed poll does. Such a method logs nothing.

items.title: Sharing code between handlers
items.text: A handler cannot be called, and self.vote(...) raises HandlerNotCallableError. Put what they share in a plain method, as _count above. To run the handler itself, call Poll.vote.func(self, ctx, 0), the plain function. It gets no injection, so pass what it injects yourself.

items.title: Which version to raise
items.text:
What changed Raise What it retires One handler's arguments The handler's version The old buttons of that handler The fields, or where the state lives The view's version Every button of every old message

If both changed, raise the view's. The class you keep at the old version holds the old handlers.

items.title: on_outdated
items.text:
View.on_outdated answers a click that reaches a class but cannot run: its handler has gone, its arguments changed, or the state no longer fits the fields. Data that looks broken, such as an id that does not parse, stays away from it: the click fails in Discord, and risa logs a line.

  • It belongs to the class the button reaches. That class is the one at the button's name and version, which is why a raised view version needs a class at the old one.
  • ctx has no view. ctx.respond and a ctx.edit with nothing to click work, and ctx.rerender() raises NoViewError.
  • Its parameters are injected, as a handler's are. Your type checker wants = risa.INJECTED on them, since the base method takes only ctx.
  • Auto-defer does not cover it. Answer within the three seconds Discord gives you.
  • By default it does nothing. The click fails in Discord. Overriding it also lowers a WARNING about a missing handler to DEBUG.

on_state_missing follows the same rules, for a record that is gone.

items.title: Several processes
items.text:
Run more than one process, and two clicks on one message can land in two places. This chapter shows when that happens, what it does to your views, and how to keep every click.

A bot in one process needs nothing from here. With several processes, put every InStore view on Redis or PostgreSQL. On a REST bot with several processes, move every view that cannot lose a click to such a store as well.

items.title: Where a click lands
items.text:
Two people click the same message. Which process runs each click depends on the kind of bot:

Gateway bot Click 1 Click 2 The guild's shard decides Process 1 Both clicks Process 2 No click All clicks on one message reach one process, so they can wait for each other there. REST bot, several processes Click 1 Click 2 The load balancer decides Process 1 Click 1 Process 2 Click 2 Each click can reach another process, so two can run at the same moment.
  • A gateway bot has several processes when you split its shards, with shard_ids and shard_count on bot.run. A message's guild decides its shard, by Discord's formula, and a DM goes to shard 0. That process need not be the one that sent the message.
  • A REST bot has several when you run several copies behind a load balancer, which picks a copy for each click.

items.title: What two clicks do to a view
items.text:
Two people click Yes at the same moment on a poll at 5, so the right result is 7:

Gateway botREST bot, several processes InMessage7Both clicks count.6Both processes read 5 and write 6, so one click is lost, and nothing logs it. InStore on Redis or PostgreSQL7Both clicks count.7Both clicks count. The second waits for the first, across the processes. InStore on MemoryStore7, until a restartBoth clicks count, and a restart loses the poll.Most clicks failOnly the process that sent the poll has its record. Elsewhere on_state_missing runs.

A click that finds no record runs on_state_missing. A REST bot with one process behaves like the gateway column. A gateway bot with split shards can miss a MemoryStore record too, when one process sends a message into a guild another process serves, and add_view warns about a MemoryStore at startup unless you made it with warn=False.

In a message, one more thing holds on every bot: a vote changes the ids, so a click that reaches Discord after the first edit fails there, and the person has to click again. In a store the ids stay.

items.title: What to set up
items.text:
A view in the message needs no store. A view in a store needs RedisStore or PostgresStore, on one server for all processes, or your own. Every process runs the same setup.

connection = redis.asyncio.Redis(host=os.environ["REDIS_HOST"])
client = risa.client_from_lightbulb(
    lightbulb_client,
    store=RedisStore(connection),
    auto_defer=risa.AutoDefer.UPDATE,
)
client.add_view(Poll)

items.title: How clicks take turns
items.text:
On Redis or PostgreSQL, clicks on one view run one after another, across processes too. Each goes through these steps:

  1. 1In-process lockOther clicks on this record in this process wait.
  2. 2LeaseAn expiring claim in the store makes clicks in other processes wait.
  3. 3The handlerIt runs on the record it read, and the lease keeps renewing.
  4. 4Compare-and-setrerender() writes only if the record is still at the version it read.

A process that crashes during step 3 blocks that view until its lease runs out, 5 seconds by default, or the lease= you give RedisStore or PostgresStore.

A click waits up to 10 seconds, then fails with an ERROR in your log. Discord's three seconds keep running meanwhile, which is why the client above sets auto-defer: it answers in time.

items.title: InMessage on a REST bot
items.text: An InMessage view has only step 1, so nothing spans the processes. Two clicks at the same moment read the same state: both raise a count from 5 to 6, and both edits say 6. The last edit wins, one click is lost, and your log shows nothing. If a view cannot lose a click, move it to a store.

items.title: When a handler loses the race
items.text:
A lease can run out under a handler that runs past max_hold, 60 seconds by default, or in a process that stalls, and a Redis failover can lose one. The next click then runs beside the first, and step 4 lets only one write through. The other's ctx.rerender() raises StateConflictError. By then self holds the state that won, so the handler can apply its change once more.

@risa.handler
async def vote_yes(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
    if not await self._first_vote(ctx):
        return
    self.yes += 1
    try:
        await ctx.rerender()
    except risa.StateConflictError:
        if await self._first_vote(ctx):
            self.yes += 1
            await ctx.rerender()

_first_vote runs again on the record that won, so someone whose vote is already in gets "You already voted."

If a process with other fields won, say during a deploy, this process cannot read the record. ctx.rerender() then raises StateUnreadableError, which this except lets through: the handler fails, risa logs it, and the vote is lost. Discord shows the click as failed, unless auto-defer answered it first.

The retry is one attempt. If it conflicts too, rerender() raises again, risa logs the error and that click fails.

Without the except, the handler fails: risa logs the error, Discord shows the click as failed unless auto-defer answered it first, and the message shows what the winner wrote. A handler that changes a field and never calls rerender() cannot catch anything, so risa logs a WARNING and drops the change.

    no: int = 0

        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"## {self.question}"),
            ui.Row(
                ui.Button(self.vote_yes, label=f"Yes: {self.yes}"),
                ui.Button(self.vote_no, label=f"No: {self.no}"),
            ),
        )

    async def vote_yes(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        if not await self._first_vote(ctx):
            return
        self.yes += 1
        try:
            await ctx.rerender()
        except risa.StateConflictError:
            if await self._first_vote(ctx):
                self.yes += 1
                await ctx.rerender()

    @risa.handler

            return
        self.no += 1

            await ctx.rerender()

            if await self._first_vote(ctx):
                self.no += 1
                await ctx.rerender()

    async def _first_vote(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> bool:
        if ctx.user.id in self.voters:
            await ctx.respond("You already voted.", ephemeral=True)

        self.voters.append(ctx.user.id)

        await ctx.edit(ui.TextDisplay("This poll has expired."))

items.title: Writing your own store
items.text: A store is six methods. Write them against what you already run, and verify_store tells you whether risa can rely on them.

items.title: The six methods
items.text:
risa.Store is a protocol, and the reference has each method in full.

Method What it has to do get_versioned(key) Return the bytes last written, unchanged, with the entry's version, as a risa.VersionedEntry, or None if the entry is missing or expired put(key, value, *, ttl) Write whether or not an entry exists, and change the version put_if_version(key, value, *, expected, ttl) Write only if the entry is at version expected, in one atomic step, and return the new version. Otherwise write nothing and return None delete(key) Remove the entry, if there is one touch(key, *, ttl) Restart the entry's lifetime, leave its data and version alone, and leave a missing key missing lock(key, *, timeout=...) Return an async context manager that holds the key exclusively and leaves other keys free. It raises risa.LockTimeoutError after waiting timeout seconds

ttl is in seconds, fractions included. None means no expiry and clears any earlier one.

A missing entry is never an error. Let every other failure raise: risa reports it as StoreUnavailableError, so an outage cannot pass for an expired view.

items.title: A minimal store
items.text:
DictStore keeps its entries in a dict. put_if_version decides whose write lands when two clicks race:

async def put_if_version(
    self,
    key: str,
    value: bytes,
    *,
    expected: int,
    ttl: float | None,
) -> int | None:
    entry = self._live(key)
    if entry is None or entry.version != expected:
        return None
    written = self._new_entry(value, ttl)
    self._entries[key] = written
    return written.version

No await sits between the compare and the write here, so nothing can run between them. A real backend needs one step of its own for this, as RedisStore has a Lua script and PostgresStore one UPDATE.

The lock is one asyncio.Lock per key:

@contextlib.asynccontextmanager
async def lock(
    self,
    key: str,
    *,
    timeout: float = risa.DEFAULT_LOCK_TIMEOUT,
) -> collections.abc.AsyncGenerator[None]:
    lock = self._locks.setdefault(key, asyncio.Lock())
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(timeout):
            await lock.acquire()
    except TimeoutError as exc:
        raise risa.LockTimeoutError(key, timeout) from exc
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        lock.release()

risa calls lock without await, as asynccontextmanager allows. A client takes the store like any other:

client = risa.client_from_app(bot, store=DictStore())
client.add_view(Tally)

"""A store of your own, and the test that holds it to what risa relies on."""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import contextlib
import itertools
import os
import time
import typing

import hikari
import msgspec

import risa
from risa import ui
from risa.store.testing import verify_store

if typing.TYPE_CHECKING:
    import collections.abc


class _Entry(msgspec.Struct):
    data: bytes
    version: int
    expires_at: float | None


class DictStore(risa.Store):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._entries: dict[str, _Entry] = {}
        self._locks: dict[str, asyncio.Lock] = {}
        self._versions = itertools.count(1)

    async def get_versioned(self, key: str) -> risa.VersionedEntry | None:
        entry = self._live(key)
        if entry is None:
            return None
        return risa.VersionedEntry(data=entry.data, version=entry.version)

    async def put(self, key: str, value: bytes, *, ttl: float | None) -> None:
        self._entries[key] = self._new_entry(value, ttl)

    async def put_if_version(
        self,
        key: str,
        value: bytes,
        *,
        expected: int,
        ttl: float | None,
    ) -> int | None:
        entry = self._live(key)
        if entry is None or entry.version != expected:
            return None
        written = self._new_entry(value, ttl)
        self._entries[key] = written
        return written.version

    async def delete(self, key: str) -> None:
        self._entries.pop(key, None)

    async def touch(self, key: str, *, ttl: float) -> None:
        entry = self._live(key)
        if entry is not None:
            entry.expires_at = time.monotonic() + ttl

    @contextlib.asynccontextmanager
    async def lock(
        self,
        key: str,
        *,
        timeout: float = risa.DEFAULT_LOCK_TIMEOUT,
    ) -> collections.abc.AsyncGenerator[None]:
        lock = self._locks.setdefault(key, asyncio.Lock())
        try:
            async with asyncio.timeout(timeout):
                await lock.acquire()
        except TimeoutError as exc:
            raise risa.LockTimeoutError(key, timeout) from exc
        try:
            yield
        finally:
            lock.release()

    def _live(self, key: str) -> _Entry | None:
        entry = self._entries.get(key)
        if entry is None or entry.expires_at is None:
            return entry
        if entry.expires_at > time.monotonic():
            return entry
        del self._entries[key]
        return None

    def _new_entry(self, value: bytes, ttl: float | None) -> _Entry:
        expires_at = None if ttl is None else time.monotonic() + ttl
        return _Entry(value, next(self._versions), expires_at)


async def test_dict_store() -> None:
    await verify_store(DictStore())


@risa.register(name="tally", state=risa.InStore(ttl=3600))
class Tally(risa.View):
    count: int = 0

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Row(ui.Button(self.add, label=f"Count: {self.count}"))

    @risa.handler
    async def add(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        self.count += 1
        await ctx.rerender()


def main() -> None:
    bot = hikari.GatewayBot(
        os.environ["DISCORD_TOKEN"],
        intents=hikari.Intents.ALL_UNPRIVILEGED | hikari.Intents.MESSAGE_CONTENT,
    )
    client = risa.client_from_app(bot, store=DictStore())
    client.add_view(Tally)

    @bot.listen()
    async def on_message(event: hikari.GuildMessageCreateEvent) -> None:
        if event.content == "!tally":
            rendered = await client.build(Tally())
            await rendered.send_to(bot.rest, event.channel_id)

    bot.run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

items.title: Test it
items.text:
Add verify_store to your tests, with a store connected to a real instance of your backend.

async def test_dict_store() -> None:
    await verify_store(DictStore())

This one needs pytest-asyncio with asyncio_mode = "auto". In a script, asyncio.run(verify_store(DictStore())) does the same. A failed check makes it raise StoreConformanceError, which lists every failure.

Try it.

Take or entry.version != expected out of put_if_version. verify_store now names a_stale_cas_is_refused and racing_cas_writes_have_one_winner.

items.title: Stores that processes share
items.text:
verify_store runs in one process, so a lock that excludes only its own process passes. For several processes, lock has to exclude all of them. Without that, two clicks run at once, and one of them gets StateConflictError.

DictStore is a teaching example, for one process only. It gets no startup warning, and it keeps every lock and every expired entry nobody reads, so a bot that runs on it grows until it restarts.

items.title: Get started
items.text:
Install risa and send your first view.

  • Installation

    Add risa to your bot, with the extras you need.

  • Your first view

    Build a counter, restart the bot and watch it keep its count.

  • Coming from miru

    Map what you know from miru onto risa, and see what risa does not have.

items.title: Coming from miru
items.text:
hikari-risa is not a direct successor to miru, so it does some things differently. Much of it will still look familiar: a view class, methods that answer clicks, a client that routes them. The big change is where a view lives. A miru view is an object in your bot's memory. A risa view is rebuilt on every click, from state kept in the message or in a store you choose.

This page compares with miru 4.3.1. The main things miru has and risa does not are under What risa does not have. risa needs Python 3.12 to 3.15, and miru 4.3.1 needs 3.11 or newer.

items.title: The same things under other names
items.text: miru risa class MyView(miru.View) @risa.register(name="my-view") above class MyView(risa.View) self.x = 0 in __init__ An annotated field, x: int = 0 An attribute set on a view stays until the view stops A risa.Prop starts from its default on every click, and load() fills it @miru.button(...) on a callback (self, ctx, button) @risa.handler on a method (self, ctx), and ui.Button(self.method, ...) in render() @miru.text_select(...) and select.values ui.TextSelect(self.method, ...) and ctx.values select.values on a miru.RoleSelect holds the roles ctx.values holds their ids, and ctx.resolved the roles miru.Button subclasses that hold a value One handler with an argument, ui.Button(risa.bind(self.method, value)) view.add_item(...) and remove_item(...) if and for in render() miru.ViewContext risa.ComponentContext ctx.view self await ctx.edit_response(components=self) await ctx.rerender() ctx.respond("Hi", flags=hikari.MessageFlag.EPHEMERAL) ctx.respond("Hi", ephemeral=True) miru.Client(bot) risa.client_from_app(bot), or risa.client_from_lightbulb(lightbulb_client) with lightbulb client.start_view(view) after each send client.add_view(MyView) once at startup respond("Hi", components=view) respond(**await client.build(MyView())) timeout=, 120 seconds by default InStore(ttl=...), and no expiry in the message autodefer=True by default, after 2 seconds AutoDefer.OFF by default; set it on a handler, view or client alluka, with @client.inject_dependencies linkd, with no decorator; Dependency injection says which parameters are injected

items.title: A view
items.text:
miru's guide to editing items has a counter. This is its counter button:

miru
class EditView(miru.View):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs) -> None:
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.counter = 0

    @miru.button(label="Counter: 0", style=hikari.ButtonStyle.PRIMARY)
    async def counter_button(
        self, ctx: miru.ViewContext, button: miru.Button
    ) -> None:
        self.counter += 1
        button.label = f"Counter: {self.counter}"
        await ctx.edit_response(components=self)

And this is a counter in risa:

risa
@risa.register(name="counter")
class Counter(risa.View):
    count: int = 0

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"Clicks: **{self.count}**"),
            ui.Row(ui.Button(self.click, label="+1")),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def click(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        self.count += 1
        await ctx.rerender()

Three things differ:

  • Items come from render(). A miru item is an object you change. A risa button is drawn again on every rerender, so you change the fields and the button follows.
  • The whole message is the view. A miru 4.3.1 view builds action rows, and you pass content and embeds beside them. A risa view renders with Components V2: containers, sections, galleries and rows. Such a message has no content, so the text goes in ui.TextDisplay.
  • There is no __init__. A view is a msgspec.Struct, made with Counter(count=3), and its annotated fields are saved from click to click. For what should not be saved, such as a database row, mark the field risa.Prop[T] and fill it in load(), which runs before every handler, as Fresh data shows.

items.title: Sending
items.text:
In miru, each message gets its own view object, which you start after sending:

miru
view = EditView()
await event.message.respond("Hello miru!", components=view)
client.start_view(view)

In risa, you add the class once. client.build renders an instance for each message, and nothing needs starting:

risa
client = risa.client_from_app(bot)
client.add_view(Counter)

@bot.listen()
async def on_message(event: hikari.GuildMessageCreateEvent) -> None:
    if event.content == "!counter":
        rendered = await client.build(Counter())
        await rendered.send_to(bot.rest, event.channel_id)

The result spreads into any call that takes components=, so inside a handler it reads await ctx.respond(**await client.build(Counter())).

items.title: Restarts
items.text:
miru's guide to persistent views says that after a restart "your views will no longer work, even if the timeout did not expire". The answer there is a persistent view: timeout=None, a custom_id on every item, and starting the view again at startup.

miru
class Persistence(miru.View):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(timeout=None)

    @miru.button(label="Button 1", custom_id="my_unique_custom_id_1")
    async def button_one(self, ctx: miru.ViewContext, button: miru.Button) -> None:
        await ctx.respond("You pressed button 1.")


@bot.listen()
async def start_views(event: hikari.StartedEvent) -> None:
    client.start_view(Persistence(), bind_to=None)

An unbound view like this one serves every message of its type and does not know which message it is on. A bound view serves one message: you pass its id, which you keep yourself, or it binds to the first message clicked. Either way, you bring back whatever the view held.

In risa, the Counter above already survives a restart. add_view at startup is the whole setup, there is no timeout=None and no custom_id, and each message keeps its own count. See Restart it for how that works.

This has costs:

  • The view's name is its route, and so is its version, which you raise when you change its fields or move it to a store. Either change retires the buttons already sent. Appending a field with a default needs no new version, and Changing a view safely lists the rest.
  • State in the message has limited room: about 60 bytes on one button, and about 70 more for each further one, with the default codec. Anyone who can see the message can read it.
  • A rerender that changes state in the message changes the id of the button that holds it, and Discord refuses a click on the old id. If two people click at nearly the same moment, the second can fail and click again. A view in a store keeps its ids unless a bound argument changes.
  • A view in a MemoryStore does not survive a restart. Use RedisStore or PostgresStore for that.

items.title: Timeouts
items.text:
A miru view times out after 120 seconds of inactivity unless you pass another timeout=. Then on_timeout() runs and the view stops.

miru
class TimeoutView(miru.View):
    @miru.button(label="Click me!", style=hikari.ButtonStyle.SUCCESS)
    async def basic_button(self, ctx: miru.ViewContext, button: miru.Button) -> None:
        await ctx.respond("You clicked me!")

    async def on_timeout(self) -> None:
        print("This view timed out!")


view = TimeoutView(timeout=10.0)

A risa view in the message has no timeout: it works as long as the message exists. For a lifetime, keep the state in a store with InStore. ttl has no default. Like miru's timeout it counts seconds of inactivity, and every click restarts it.

risa
@risa.register(name="question", state=risa.InStore(ttl=600))
class Question(risa.View):
    text: str

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(self.text),
            ui.Row(ui.Button(self.yes, label="Yes")),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def yes(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        await ctx.edit(ui.TextDisplay(f"{self.text} **Yes.**"))

    @classmethod
    async def on_state_missing(cls, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        await ctx.respond("This question has expired.", ephemeral=True)

The client needs a store for this. A MemoryStore needs nothing installed, and it forgets everything when the bot restarts:

client = risa.client_from_app(bot, store=risa.MemoryStore())
client.add_view(Question)

on_timeout() runs when the time is up. risa has no timer, so on_state_missing() runs when someone clicks after the record has expired. Until then the message stays as it is, and risa has no hook for greying out its buttons at that moment.

To end a view yourself, where miru has self.stop(), replace the message with a layout that has no buttons. yes above does that with ctx.edit.

items.title: What risa does not have
items.text:
• Modals. miru has modals, with miru.Modal and ctx.respond_with_modal. risa's are designed but not built, because they wait for hikari to parse Discord's new modal components.
  • Menus and navigators. miru ships miru.ext.menu and miru.ext.nav. In risa you write these yourself, for example as a view with a page: int field.
  • A check before every handler. miru has view_check. In risa, a handler checks ctx.user itself.
  • An error hook on each view. miru has on_error on each view. risa has error handlers for the whole client, and a handler that wants its own answer uses try.
  • Waiting on a view. miru has view.wait() and wait_for_input(). A risa view has no object that lives between clicks, so the code you would run after wait() goes in the handler.
  • Sharing injection with arc. miru has Client.from_arc. risa shares a dependency manager with lightbulb only, through client_from_lightbulb. With arc or crescent, make the client with client_from_app.

items.title: Moving one view at a time
items.text:
A bot can run both, so you need not move everything at once. A risa client answers only the ids risa wrote.

On a gateway bot, make the miru client with ignore_unknown_interactions=True. Without it, miru logs a warning for every click on a risa view.

On a REST bot, hikari has one slot for a component listener, so make the miru client first. risa takes the slot and passes on each click it does not handle, and it logs a warning about that unless you pass warn_shared_listener=False. In the other order, miru's own call to set its listener raises.

items.title: Your first view
items.text: Build a counter: one message with one button, where each click raises the number. It runs on your own bot and keeps counting after a restart.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• Install hikari-risa.
  • Create an application in Discord's Developer Portal and copy the token from its Bot page.
  • Invite the bot to a server you can test in, with the scopes bot and applications.commands and the permission to send messages.
  • Put the token in the environment variable DISCORD_TOKEN:
export DISCORD_TOKEN="your-bot-token"

In Windows PowerShell, that is $env:DISCORD_TOKEN = "your-bot-token".

items.title: The view
items.text:
A view is a class. Its fields are its state, render() draws the message from them, and its handlers answer the clicks.

@risa.register(name="counter")
class Counter(risa.View):
    count: int = 0

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"Clicks: **{self.count}**"),
            ui.Row(ui.Button(self.click, label="+1")),
        )

    @risa.handler
    async def click(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        self.count += 1
        await ctx.rerender()

Part by part:

  • @risa.register(name="counter") tells risa about the class. A click finds its way back to the view by this name, so keep the name once messages are out. Renaming a view retires the buttons already sent.
  • count: int = 0 is the state. risa keeps every annotated field from click to click, and the default is where a new counter starts.
  • render() returns the message's layout, drawn from the fields. ui.Container is a box like an embed, ui.TextDisplay is text in Discord's markdown, and ui.Row holds buttons. Selects, sections, galleries shows everything else you can draw.
  • ui.Button(self.click, label="+1") draws a button, and self.click is the handler its clicks go to.
  • @risa.handler makes click a handler. When it runs, the view already holds the state from the click, and ctx is the context of that click.
  • await ctx.rerender() answers the click: it draws the message again from the changed fields and saves them. Discord fails a click that gets no answer within three seconds.

items.title: Send it
items.text:
A view reaches Discord in two steps. Once at startup, you make a client and give it the class with add_view, so that clicks find it. Then, for each message, client.build(Counter()) renders a new view and you send the result.

The two ways below differ in what makes the bot post. Pick one.

lightbulbGateway

/counter posts the counter. Take this one if your bot gets its slash commands from lightbulb. You install it yourself, with uv add hikari-lightbulb or pip install hikari-lightbulb. The metadata of hikari-lightbulb 3.2.6 declares Python below 3.15.

risa_client = risa.client_from_lightbulb(lightbulb_client)
risa_client.add_view(Counter)

@lightbulb_client.register()
class CounterCommand(
    lightbulb.SlashCommand,
    name="counter",
    description="Post the counter.",
):
    @lightbulb.invoke
    async def invoke(self, ctx: lightbulb.Context) -> None:
        await ctx.respond(**await risa_client.build(Counter()))

risa.client_from_lightbulb makes a client that shares lightbulb's bot and its dependency manager. build returns a mapping, and ** spreads it into ctx.respond. lightbulb registers /counter with Discord when the bot starts.

"""The counter, sent from a lightbulb slash command."""

from __future__ import annotations

import os

import hikari
import lightbulb

import risa
from risa import ui


@risa.register(name="counter")

    count: int = 0

    def render(self) -> ui.Layout:
        return ui.Container(
            ui.TextDisplay(f"Clicks: **{self.count}**"),
            ui.Row(ui.Button(self.click, label="+1")),
        )

    async def click(self, ctx: risa.ComponentContext) -> None:
        self.count += 1
        await ctx.rerender()


def main() -> None:
    bot = hikari.GatewayBot(os.environ["DISCORD_TOKEN"])
    lightbulb_client = lightbulb.client_from_app(bot)
    bot.subscribe(hikari.StartingEvent, lightbulb_client.start)

    risa_client = risa.client_from_lightbulb(lightbulb_client)
    risa_client.add_view(Counter)

    @lightbulb_client.register()

        lightbulb.SlashCommand,
        name="counter",
        description="Post the counter.",
    ):
        @lightbulb.invoke
        async def invoke(self, ctx: lightbulb.Context) -> None:
            await ctx.respond(**await risa_client.build(Counter()))

    bot.run()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Reading what people write takes a privileged intent. Turn on Message Content Intent on the Bot page of the Developer Portal, or Discord closes the connection when the bot starts.

items.title: Run it
items.text:
Save the full file of your tab as bot.py and start it:

uv run bot.py

If you installed with pip, that is python bot.py. Post the counter the way your tab does, then click +1. The number in the message goes up.

items.title: Restart it
items.text:
Stop the bot with Ctrl+C, start it again, and click +1 on the same message. The count carries on.

The count is not kept in your bot. When risa draws the button, it writes the count into the button's hidden id, which Discord stores with the message and sends back with every click. On a click, risa reads the count out of the message, rebuilds the view and runs your handler, and ctx.rerender() writes the new count onto the button. A restart loses nothing, and the new process only needs add_view, which your code calls at every start.

A click that lands while the bot is down fails in Discord, which shows that the interaction failed. The count stays where it was, and the next click after the restart works.

The count is not secret.

Anyone who can see the message can read what the button holds, so keep secrets somewhere else.

The message also has limited room: about 60 bytes on one button, and about 70 more for each further one, with the default codec. A view that needs more can move to a store with risa.InStore. Its handlers stay the same, but the move means raising its version, which retires the buttons already sent.

A click changes the id of the button that holds the count, and Discord refuses a click on an id the message no longer has. If two people click at nearly the same moment, the second can fail in Discord and click again. In a store the ids hold a key instead of the count, so clicks leave them as they are, which suits a view many people click at once.

In miru.

A view stops answering after a restart unless you make it persistent. Coming from miru has the whole comparison.

Try it.

Add a button that subtracts one: a second @risa.handler with self.count -= 1, and a second ui.Button in the row. Restart the bot and click +1 on the old message. It keeps its count and gains the new button.

items.title: Installation
items.text: Add hikari-risa to your bot's project. It runs on Python 3.12 to 3.15, and you import it as risa.

items.title: Install
items.text:
uvpip 
uv add hikari-risa

pip install hikari-risa

This also installs what risa depends on: hikari, linkd and msgspec. uv add needs a project to add to, so run uv init first if you have no pyproject.toml yet.

Run hikari-risa to check that it worked. It prints the version of risa, where it is installed and the versions of Python and of what risa installs; paste that into a bug report.

uvpip 
uv run hikari-risa

hikari-risa

python -m risa does the same, and hikari-risa --version prints only the version.

items.title: Extras
items.text:
A view keeps its state in its message by default, and that needs nothing extra. Three extras add more:

Extra Installs You want it when redis redis Your views keep their state in Redis, with RedisStore. postgres asyncpg Your views keep their state in PostgreSQL, with PostgresStore. radixly radixly A view runs out of room in its message. The codecs BASE32768 and URO14 fit more than twice as much.

Name one when you install:

uvpip 
uv add "hikari-risa[redis]"

pip install "hikari-risa[redis]"

items.title: Packages your bot may need
items.text:
Two more packages depend on how your bot runs, and hikari-risa installs neither:

  • A bot with slash commands through lightbulb needs hikari-lightbulb.
  • A REST bot needs hikari[server], because hikari's interaction server checks Discord's signatures with it.
